This uncontrolled movement of air can also carry moisture to cold surfaces where it can condense. In hot humid climates outdoor air can condense on the air-conditioning equipment and ductwork typically located in attic spaces; in cold climates warm indoor air leaking into the attic can condense against the underside of the roof sheathing.  
Durability – Openings in the soffits, gables, mushroom and ridge vents allow more than just air to enter the attic. In cold northern climates snow can be blown in through these openings, accumulating, melting and causing damage to the ceiling or creating the potential premature structural failure or mold growth inside the roof assembly. In coastal climates wind driven rain can be blown in through these openings with similar results. In areas subject to wildfires, burning embers can be blown in through these openings, potentially starting roof fires.
Why Use Closed-Cell Spray Polyurethane Foam (ccSPF)?
Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam can be used to create an unvented roof assembly that works in all climate zones. The design approach is the same for all climate zones.
There are currently two types of spray polyurethane foam (SPF) insulation used in North American residential construction:  ccSPF or closed-cell medium-density spray foam (”2 pound” or 2 pounds per cubic foot) and ocSPF or open-cell low-density spray foam (“half pound” or 0.5 pcf). When installed properly, both adhere to most construction surfaces and expand to fill voids and create an air seal. Closed-cell spray foam made with EPA-approved HFC blowing agents like, Honeywell Enovate 245fa, has a higher thermal resistance (e.g. is a better insulation) and lower vapor permeance than open-cell spray foam. Closed-cell spray foam acts as an air barrier (at 1 in. or 25 mm minimum thickness) and vapor retarder (at 2 in. or 50 mm minimum thickness*) and therefore does not need an additional vapor retarder in cold climates).
Unvented roof assemblies with ccSPF work well in all climate zones and serve several important functions:
Controls Airflow – ccSPF is air impermeable, adheres well to almost all construction surfaces and expands to fill voids creating an air seal and eliminating air leakage. In cold climates it prevents warm, humid indoor air from reaching the back (underside) of roof sheathing where it can condense. In warm climates it prevents humid outside air that enters the roof due to natural and/or controlled ventilation from reaching the back of the roof sheathing, which can be cooled below the air temperature by night sky radiation (i.e. the effect that causes dew).
Control Heat Flow – Closed-cell spray foam has exceptional thermal performance relative to other insulations (i.e. the highest R-value per inch.) ccSPF can be used to create a very compact roof assembly that meets or exceeds the code required thermal performance.
Control Vapor Diffusion – Closed-cell spray foam acts as a throttle to control the rate of vapor diffusion. The foam insulation resists the diffusion of water vapor so that the amount of water vapor is reduced as it moves through the thickness of the foam. By the time the water vapor reaches the back of the roof sheathing, there is not enough left to cause condensation problems.
In cold climates the ccSPF provides the first condensing plane. The ccSPF should be installed directly to the face (i.e. back) of the roof sheathing in a layer thick enough to prevent condensation from forming on the inside face of the foam.
In hot climates up to 5 in.* (125 mm) of ccSPF can also be used. In this application the assembly can still dry to the inside during the daytime when roof temperatures are high (120-190°F or 50-90°C), the vapor pressure gradients are very large (5-35 kPa) and the foam is a vapor retarder and not a vapor barrier.
Controls Rain Leakage – Closed-cell spray foam has negligible water permeability, minimal water absorption, and excellent adhesion allowing it to act as a secondary rainwater barrier to limit damage when primary roof assembly rainwater control membranes leak. Rainwater migration is severely limited due to the low water transmission and high adhesion (“waterproofing”) characteristics of the foam and damage is limited to the area immediately adjacent the hole in the primary rainwater control membrane. This tends to contain the damage, making it easier to identify the source and preventing it from spreading throughout the assembly and to interior finishes which can be costly to repair.
Closed-cell medium-density spray polyurethane foam (ccSPF) insulation can be used to create an unvented roof assembly for any climate zone. Be sure to:
Control vapor diffusion – The inherent characteristics of the ccSPF allow it to be used in all climate zones without requiring the installation of any additional vapor diffusion control (i.e. no additional vapor retarder layer or coating is required with ccSPF installed to thicknesses greater than about 2 in. or 50mm*).
* Consult the specific manufacturer’s application instructions and technical data sheet for maximum allowable thickness and minimum thickness required to qualify as a suitable vapor retarder.

BSD-102 Snippet:
 BSD-102: Understanding Attic Ventilation
Joseph Lstiburek
Effective Date
October 25, 2006
Abstract

Attics or roofs can be designed and constructed to be either vented or unvented in any hygro-thermal zone (Map 1). The choice of venting or not venting is a design and construction choice not a requirement determined by the physics or by the building code. The model building codes allow both vented and unvented roof assemblies. The applicable physics impacts the design of attic or roof systems as does the applicable building code but neither limit the choice.

Text

 

Throughout the balance of this digest the terms attic and roof will and can be used interchangeably.

In cold climates, the primary purpose of attic or roof ventilation is to maintain a cold roof temperature to control ice dams created by melting snow, and to vent moisture that moves from the conditioned space to the attic (ventilation acts to bypass the vapour barrier created by most roof membranes). Melted snow, in this case, is caused by heat loss from the conditioned space. The heat loss is typically a combination of air leakage and conductive losses. The air leakage is due to exfiltration from the conditioned space (often because a ceiling air barrier is not present) and from leaky supply ductwork (often because ductwork located in attics is not well sealed) and from penetrations like non-airtight recessed lights. The conductive losses are usually from supply ductwork and equipment located in attic spaces ab

const memoText = `DECISION MEMO: CLIMATE-CONTROLLED SHED INSULATION STRATEGIES
Target Structure: 10x12 Backyard Office / Workshop (120 sq. ft. Footprint, 590 sq. ft. Total Thermal Envelope)

1. EXECUTIVE DECISION SUMMARY
- BEST OVERALL OPTION: Strategy 2 - Mineral Wool (Rockwool Comfortbatt) + Continuous Rigid Foam Hybrid
  Why: Delivers superior thermal and acoustic performance (R-15 walls, R-25 ceiling, R-10 floor). Rockwool is noncombustible, hydrophobic (does not slump or rot when exposed to humidity), and friction-fits tightly. Continuous 2" XPS rigid foam on the ceiling breaks thermal bridging across rafters and forms an airtight vapor-retarder plane that stops warm indoor moisture from reaching the roof deck. Completely DIY-friendly with hand tools; zero hazardous chemical off-gassing. Material Cost: ~$1,154.

- BEST BUDGET OPTION: Strategy 1 - Traditional Vented Fiberglass Batt Assembly
  Why: Uses standard R-13 kraft-faced fiberglass in 2x4 walls, R-19 in 2x6 ceiling rafters with plastic ventilation baffles (Accuvent/Durovent), and R-13 in floor joists over a 6-mil poly ground barrier. Lowest upfront cost (~$485 - $550).
  Trade-offs: Moderate R-value, vulnerable to airflow degradation, slumps and harbors mold if exposed to moisture, attractive to rodents, and requires meticulous stapling and air sealing.

- OPTION TO AVOID: Strategy 3 - DIY Closed-Cell Spray Foam Kits (Froth-Pak / Touch 'n Foam)
  Why Avoid: Prohibitively expensive ($2,574 - $3,003 for 6-7 Froth-Pak 200 kits), high risk of catastrophic DIY application failure (substrate temperature sensitivity causes off-ratio chemical mixing, leaving gooey, foul-smelling, toxic un-cured foam that must be hand-scraped), exothermic fire hazard if sprayed >2" in a single pass, severe isocyanate fumes requiring full chemical PPE and respirators, and permanently conceals roof deck water leaks until structural rot occurs.

2. DETAILED COMPARISON OF 3 FULL INSULATION STRATEGIES

STRATEGY 1: Budget Fiberglass Batts with Vented Roof (Traditional Cavity Fill)
- Walls: 2x4 framing with R-13 kraft-faced fiberglass rolls/batts.
- Roof/Ceiling: 2x6 rafters with rafter baffles (1" air chute beneath deck) and R-19 fiberglass batts.
- Floor: 2x6 joists with R-13 batts held by wire stays + 6-mil poly ground vapor barrier.
- R-Value Approach: Walls R-13, Ceiling R-19, Floor R-13.
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Kraft paper facing on warm-in-winter side; soffit-to-ridge ventilation baffles prevent warm moist indoor exfiltration from condensing on the cold roof deck.
- Interior Space Consumed: 0" (sits flush inside stud and rafter cavities).
- DIY Difficulty: Low / Beginner (standard utility knife and stapler).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Fiberglass loses R-value if compressed or wet; crushed baffles cause roof deck rot; rodent nesting in floor cavities.

STRATEGY 2: Mineral Wool + Continuous Rigid Foam Hybrid (Recommended Winner)
- Walls: 2x4 framing filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt (3.5" friction-fit).
- Roof/Ceiling: Rafters filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt + continuous 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) fastened across rafter bottoms with Go Board washers/screws; seams taped with Tyvek/Sika tape and perimeter spray-foamed.
- Floor: 2x6 joists with 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) friction-fit between joists and sealed with canned foam, under 3/4" subfloor, plus 6-mil ground poly barrier.
- R-Value Approach: Walls R-15, Ceiling R-25 (R-15 batt + R-10 continuous XPS), Floor R-10.
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Rockwool is naturally hydrophobic; taped 2" rigid foam acts as an interior air barrier and Class II vapor retarder (<1.0 perm), eliminating condensation on framing.
- Interior Space Consumed: 2" loss of ceiling headroom; 0" loss on walls and floor.
- DIY Difficulty: Moderate (serrated insulation knife, straightedge for foam scoring, screw gun, seam taping).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Incomplete seam taping or perimeter foaming can allow air bypass; requires proper screw and washer spacing into rafters.

STRATEGY 3: Full Closed-Cell Spray Polyurethane Foam (ccSPF)
- Walls: 2" ccSPF sprayed directly onto exterior sheathing inside 2x4 bays (R-12.4).
- Roof/Ceiling: 3" ccSPF sprayed directly to the underside of the roof deck creating an unvented hot roof (R-18.6).
- Floor: 2" ccSPF sprayed into joist bays against subfloor (R-12.4).
- R-Value Approach: R-6.2 per inch. Walls R-12.4 (2"), Ceiling R-18.6 (3"), Floor R-12.4 (2").
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Self-flashing, air-impermeable, Class II vapor retarder at >=2" thickness. No ventilation chutes needed.
- Interior Space Consumed: 0" beyond framing cavity.
- DIY Difficulty: High / Hazardous (strict 65-80 deg F chemical temperature, full hazmat suit, organic vapor respirator, rapid 30-sec tip curing).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Off-ratio chemical mix results in toxic uncured goo; fire hazard from exothermic heat in thick passes; traps external leaks behind foam causing hidden roof deck decay.

3. PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION FOR A 10x12 CLIMATE-CONTROLLED SHED
- Wall Assembly: 2x4 framing @ 16" O.C. filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt (3.5" thickness), covered with interior 1/2" drywall or painted plywood.
- Roof/Ceiling Assembly: 2x6 rafters with upper vent chutes, filled with R-15 Rockwool batts, capped along rafter undersides by 2" Owens Corning Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) held by Go Board washers and 3" screws. All board seams taped with acrylic tape and perimeter-sealed with Great Stuff Window & Door foam, creating an airtight R-25 ceiling envelope.
- Floor Assembly: 2x6 pressure-treated floor framing set on skids/piers over a 6-mil polyethylene ground moisture sheet. 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) installed between joists and sealed at edges with canned foam; 3/4" tongue-and-groove OSB subfloor glued with construction adhesive.
- Climate Control Compatibility: Perfectly paired with a 9,000 BTU mini-split heat pump to maintain year-round temperature and actively dehumidify the conditioned space.

4. MATERIALS BASKET & ESTIMATED COST BREAKDOWN (10x12 SHED: 590 SQ. FT.)
- Strategy 1 (Budget Fiberglass):
  * Walls: 8 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced (40 sq ft/roll @ $27.97) = $223.76
  * Ceiling: 4 rolls Owens Corning R-19 Faced (~$35.00/roll) + 12 Accuvent Baffles ($5.98 ea) = $140.00 + $71.76 = $211.76
  * Floor: 3 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced ($83.91) + 6-mil poly ($22.00) + insulation wire stays ($18.00) = $123.91
  * Accessories: Staples and tape = $25.00

- Strategy 2 (Mineral Wool + Rigid Foam Hybrid - WINNER):
  * Walls: 6 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt (59.7 sq ft/bag @ $84.98) = $509.88
  * Ceiling: 3 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt ($254.94) + 5 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet = $299.85) = $554.79
  * Floor: 4 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet) = $239.88 + 6-mil poly ($22.00) = $261.88
  * Accessories: 2 cans Great Stuff Pro ($16.00), 1 roll Tyvek/Sika seam tape ($14.97), 1 box Go Board washers & screws ($24.00) = $54.97
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$1,381.52

- Strategy 3 (Full Closed-Cell Spray Foam Kit):
  * Board Feet Required: (320 sq ft walls * 2") + (120 sq ft floor * 2") + (150 sq ft ceiling * 3") = 1,330 board-ft.
  * Froth-Pak 200 Kits Required: 1,330 / 200 = 7 kits @ $429.00 = $3,003.00 (or 6 kits for 2" ceiling = $2,574.00)

  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$2,694.00 - $3,123.00

(Before and After Heating Costs)"* - **URL:** `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXeRLx9p5Oo` - **Core Findings:** Evaluates transitioning a shed roof from R-10 (2" continuous rigid foam) to R-25 (Rockwool R-15 batts in rafter bays + 2" continuous rigid foam underneath). Measured real-world heating data showing an approximate 20% reduction in daily kilowatt-hour consumption. Demonstrates fastener spacing, Go Board washers, low-expansion Great Stuff Window & Door foam, and high-bond seam tape (Sika / Tyvek) to create an airtight interior thermal lid that breaks thermal bridging across rafters. 2. **Everyday Home Repairs / Everyday Shed** — *"Most Homeowners Insulate Shed Roofs WRONG (Do This Instead)"* - **URL:** `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2uixLIvv4H0` - **Core Findings:** Demonstrates why stuffing fiberglass batts directly against an unvented shed roof deck is the #1 failure mode in DIY shed conversions (leads to interstitial condensation, mold, and rot). Shows how to fasten 2" 4x8 rigid foam panels across the bottom of rafters while maintaining an unobstructed ventilation path from soffits to ridge or upper gable vents. 3. **SethCraft Shop** — *"Insulation for Walls and Ceiling 10x12 Building"* - **URL:** `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z3q2d5SXZ7w` - **Core Findings:** Documents insulating a 10x12 detached office/workshop. Uses R-13 fiberglass batts in 2x4 wall framing and R-19 fiberglass batts in 2x6 ceiling framing. Stresses the critical requirement of installing continuous plastic rafter baffles/chutes to guarantee airflow above the ceiling batts, and integrates a ductless mini-split heat pump to actively regulate conditioned air and dehumidify the interior. 4. **SethCraft Shop** — *"How to Build an Insulated Shed Floor 10x12 Workshop"* - **URL:** `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sFC_bEAR9fQ` - **Core Findings:** Shows foundation and floor construction for a 10x12 office on treated 2x6 framing. Insulates floor cavities with 2" rigid foam board rated at R-10, lays 6-mil polyethylene ground plastic beneath the building on paver blocks to stop rising ground vapor, and glues 3/4" OSB subfloor with construction adhesive to eliminate deflection and squeaks. 5. **Everyday Shed** — *"#1 Insulation Mistake DIYers Always Regret"* - **URL:** `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kbWE0lz4QE0` - **Core Findings:** Details proper air-sealing steps prior to placing batts, highlighting Rockwool stone wool cutting/installation techniques (friction-fit, fire safety, water repellency) and the hazards of misplaced interior poly vapor barriers that trap moisture inside walls. ### B. Building Science & Manufacturer Technical Guidance (4 Non-Video Sources) 6. **Building Science Corporation (BSC) — BSD-149:** *"Unvented Roof Assemblies for All Climates"* by Christopher Schumacher - **URL:** `https://buildingscience.com/documents/digests/bsd-149-unvented-roof-assemblies-for-all-climates` - **Core Guidance:** Analyzes unvented roof physics. Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam (ccSPF) acts as an air barrier at a minimum 1" thickness and as a Class II vapor retarder at a minimum 2" thickness (<1.0 perm). Establishes that in unvented roof assemblies, the insulation directly against the sheathing must prevent the interior air from reaching dew point on the roof deck. 7. **Building Science Corporation (BSC) — BSD-102:** *"Understanding Attic Ventilation"* by Dr. Joseph Lstiburek - **URL:** `https://buildingscience.com/documents/digests/bsd-102-understanding-attic-ventilation` - **Core Guidance:** Outlines the core thermodynamic purposes of roof venting: evacuating indoor moisture exfiltration in cold seasons to prevent condensation beneath cold roof membranes and mitigating solar radiant heat load in warm seasons. Confirms both vented and unvented assemblies can succeed if air barrier and moisture boundaries are rigorously aligned. 8. **ROCKWOOL North America Technical Data:** *Comfortbatt® Stone Wool Insulation* - **URL:** `https://www.rockwool.com/north-america/products/comfortbatt/` - **Core Guidance:** R-15 for 3.5" (2x4) cavities; R-23 for 5.5" (2x6) cavities. Noncombustible (withstands up to 2,150°F), hydrophobic (does not absorb bulk water, retains R-value when exposed to humidity), mold/rot resistant, and provides high acoustic dampening. Features flexible compression edges for friction-fit installation without stapling or slumping over time. 9. **Green Building Advisor (GBA):** *"Building a 120 sq. ft. portable office: Insulation/assembly details?"* - **URL:** `https://www.greenbuildingadvisor.com/question/building-120-sq-ft-portable-office-insulation-assembly-details` - **Core Guidance:** Consensus guidance for small 10x12 detached offices: recommends rigid foam board in floor framing (or over subfloor) to avoid moisture absorption and rodent intrusion common with fiberglass; advises that if batts are used in the roof, a vented cavity with baffles is mandatory unless rigid foam or spray foam is applied continuously. ### C. Very forgiving dry installation. | **Moderate.** Mineral wool cuts cleanly with a serrated knife and friction-fits without stapling; rigid foam requires straightedge scoring, screw/washer fastening overhead, and seam taping. | **High / Hazardous.** Requires substrate/tank temperatures strictly between 65°F–80°F, full chemical PPE (organic vapor respirator, Tyvek suit, goggles), fast 30-second nozzle change discipline, and 24–48 hour off-gassing evacuation. | | **Failure Risks & Watch-Outs** | • Air leakage around batts degrades effective R-value by up to 30%.
• Slumps or absorbs water if roof leaks or humidity condenses, leading to hidden mold.
• Rodents frequently tunnel and nest in floor/wall fiberglass.
• Crushed or missing rafter baffles trap moisture, causing rapid roof deck rot. | • Unsealed board joints or perimeter gaps create convective bypass loops.
• Requires adequate screw/washer fastening so ceiling panels do not sag.
• Slightly higher material cost than entry-level fiberglass. | • Off-ratio chemical mix produces sticky, foul-smelling, toxic un-cured goo that never sets and requires manual scraping.
• Single passes >2" create extreme exothermic heat and fire hazards.
• Toxic isocyanate fumes.
• Permanently conceals exterior roof leaks until wood sheathing rots from the outside in.
• Extremely high kit cost. | *(All entries derived from reviewed field installations and technical specifications; missing parameters are noted as 'not shown' where applicable).* --- ## 3. Practical Recommendation for a 10x12 Climate-Controlled Shed For a standard 10x12 outbuilding (120 sq. ft. floor, ~320 net sq. ft. walls, ~150 sq. ft. roof/ceiling), the ideal year-round climate-controlled assembly that balances thermal resistance, airtightness, acoustic isolation, and DIY buildability is **Strategy 2 (Mineral Wool + Rigid Foam Hybrid)**. ### A. Recommended Wall Assembly - **Framing:** Standard 2x4 framing at 16" on-center. - **Exterior Weather Barrier:** Exterior sheathing (OSB or plywood) wrapped with a water-resistive barrier (DuPont Tyvek HomeWrap) with taped seams, behind standard siding on rainscreen furring strips (or direct-applied siding). - **Cavity Insulation:** **ROCKWOOL Comfortbatt R-15** (3.5" thickness, 15" width). Friction-fit firmly between studs with no gaps or compression. - **Interior Finish:** 1/2" drywall (taped and primed with vapor-retardant latex paint) or 1/2" interior plywood. An interior 6-mil poly sheet should be **omitted** to prevent a double vapor barrier that traps summer humidity. ### B. Recommended Roof / Ceiling Assembly - **Framing:** 2x6 roof rafters at 16" or 24" on-center. - **Ventilation:** Continuous vented soffit at the eaves connected to upper gable louvers or a continuous ridge vent. Install **Amerimax Accuvent** baffles (or Durovent) in every rafter bay against the roof deck to guarantee a 1" to 1.5" continuous air channel. - **Cavity Insulation:** **ROCKWOOL Comfortbatt R-15** installed below the baffles within the rafter bays. - **Continuous Thermal Break & Air Barrier:** **2" Owens Corning FOAMULAR NGX F-250 XPS (R-10)** panels fastened directly across the underside of the rafters using 3" construction screws through 1.25" Go Board / plastic insulation washers. - **Air Sealing:** Seal all board perimeter perimeters and penetrations with low-expansion Great Stuff Pro Window & Door polyurethane foam, and tape all board butt-joints with DuPont Tyvek Acrylic Construction Tape. This creates an airtight, continuous interior ceiling plane providing **R-25 total resistance** and completely stopping warm, humid indoor air from reaching the cold roof deck. ### C. Recommended Floor Assembly - **Sub-Base:** Ground cleared and sloped away from the shed, covered with a heavy **6-mil polyethylene sheet** ballasted with gravel to stop rising ground moisture. Pier blocks or skids elevate the shed floor framing at least 6" off the ground for cross-ventilation. - **Framing:** Pressure-treated 2x6 floor joists at 16" on-center. - **Insulation:** **2" Owens Corning FOAMULAR NGX XPS (R-10)** rigid foam boards cut to width and friction-fitted between the joists, supported by 1x2 ledger strips or corrosion-resistant screws. Seal all perimeter gaps between foam and joists with canned expanding foam to block air infiltration and rodent intrusion. - **Subfloor:** 3/4" tongue-and-groove exterior-grade OSB or plywood glued to the joists with subfloor construction adhesive (e.g., Liquid Nails) and screwed down. - **Finished Floor:** Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) with integrated waterproof underlayment. ### D. Climate Control Pairing Pair this tight envelope with an appropriately sized **9,000 BTU mini-split heat pump** (or a dual-hose inverter window heat pump). In a 120 sq. ft. space with an R-15/R-25/R-10 envelope, a mini-split will operate at minimum modulation, maintain exact workspace temperatures in sub-freezing winters or hot summers, and actively dehumidify the air to eliminate indoor moisture accumulation. --- ## 4. Total Envelope) *Envelope breakdown: Floor = 120 sq. ft. | Walls (net of door/windows) = 320 sq. ft. | Roof/Ceiling = 150 sq. ft.* ### Strategy 1: Budget Fiberglass Batts with Vented Roof - **Walls:** 8 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced (40 sq. ft./roll @ $27.97) = **$223.76** - <untrusted_web_content source="repl">

Full text length: 10319
Relevant lines sample:
 BSD-149: Unvented Roof Assemblies for All Climates
This uncontrolled movement of air can also carry moisture to cold surfaces where it can condense. In hot humid climates outdoor air can condense on the air-conditioning equipment and ductwork typically located in attic spaces; in cold climates warm indoor air leaking into the attic can condense against the underside of the roof sheathing.  
Durability – Openings in the soffits, gables, mushroom and ridge vents allow more than just air to enter the attic. In cold northern climates snow can be blown in through these openings, accumulating, melting and causing damage to the ceiling or creating the potential premature structural failure or mold growth inside the roof assembly. In coastal climates wind driven rain can be blown in through these openings with similar results. In areas subject to wildfires, burning embers can be blown in through these openings, potentially starting roof fires.
Why Use Closed-Cell Spray Polyurethane Foam (ccSPF)?
Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam can be used to create an unvented roof assembly that works in all climate zones. The design approach is the same for all climate zones.
There are currently two types of spray polyurethane foam (SPF) insulation used in North American residential construction:  ccSPF or closed-cell medium-density spray foam (”2 pound” or 2 pounds per cubic foot) and ocSPF or open-cell low-density spray foam (“half pound” or 0.5 pcf). When installed properly, both adhere to most construction surfaces and expand to fill voids and create an air seal. Closed-cell spray foam made with EPA-approved HFC blowing agents like, Honeywell Enovate 245fa, has a higher thermal resistance (e.g. is a better insulation) and lower vapor permeance than open-cell spray foam. Closed-cell spray foam acts as an air barrier (at 1 in. or 25 mm minimum thickness) and vapor retarder (at 2 in. or 50 mm minimum thickness*) and therefore does not need an additional vapor retarder in cold climates).
Unvented roof assemblies with ccSPF work well in all climate zones and serve several important functions:
Controls Airflow – ccSPF is air impermeable, adheres well to almost all construction surfaces and expands to fill voids creating an air seal and eliminating air leakage. In cold climates it prevents warm, humid indoor air from reaching the back (underside) of roof sheathing where it can condense. In warm climates it prevents humid outside air that enters the roof due to natural and/or controlled ventilation from reaching the back of the roof sheathing, which can be cooled below the air temperature by night sky radiation (i.e. the effect that causes dew).
Control Heat Flow – Closed-cell spray foam has exceptional thermal performance relative to other insulations (i.e. the highest R-value per inch.) ccSPF can be used to create a very compact roof assembly that meets or exceeds the code required thermal performance.
Control Vapor Diffusion – Closed-cell spray foam acts as a throttle to control the rate of vapor diffusion. The foam insulation resists the diffusion of water vapor so that the amount of water vapor is reduced as it moves through the thickness of the foam. By the time the water vapor reaches the back of the roof sheathing, there is not enough left to cause condensation problems.
In cold climates the ccSPF provides the first condensing plane. The ccSPF should be installed directly to the face (i.e. back) of the roof sheathing in a layer thick enough to prevent condensation from forming on the inside face of the foam.
In hot climates up to 5 in.* (125 mm) of ccSPF can also be used. In this application the assembly can still dry to the inside during the daytime when roof temperatures are high (120-190°F or 50-90°C), the vapor pressure gradients are very large (5-35 kPa) and the foam is a vapor retarder and not a vapor barrier.
Controls Rain Leakage – Closed-cell spray foam has negligible water permeability, minimal water absorption, and excellent adhesion allowing it to act as a secondary rainwater barrier to limit damage when primary roof assembly rainwater control membranes leak. Rainwater migration is severely limited due to the low water transmission and high adhesion (“waterproofing”) characteristics of the foam and damage is limited to the area immediately adjacent the hole in the primary rainwater control membrane. This tends to contain the damage, making it easier to identify the source and preventing it from spreading throughout the assembly and to interior finishes which can be costly to repair.
Closed-cell medium-density spray polyurethane foam (ccSPF) insulation can be used to create an unvented roof assembly for any climate zone. Be sure to:
Control vapor diffusion – The inherent characteristics of the ccSPF allow it to be used in all climate zones without requiring the installation of any additional vapor diffusion control (i.e. no additional vapor retarder layer or coating is required with ccSPF installed to thicknesses greater than about 2 in. or 50mm*).
* Consult the specific manufacturer’s application instructions and technical data sheet for maximum allowable thickness and minimum thickness required to qualify as a suitable vapor retarder.
</untrusted_web_content>

BSD-102 Title: BSD-102: Understanding Attic Ventilation | buildingscience.com
BSD-102 Snippet:
 BSD-102: Understanding Attic Ventilation
Joseph Lstiburek
Effective Date
October 25, 2006
Abstract

Attics or roofs can be designed and constructed to be either vented or unvented in any hygro-thermal zone (Map 1). The choice of venting or not venting is a design and construction choice not a requirement determined by the physics or by the building code. The model building codes allow both vented and unvented roof assemblies. The applicable physics impacts the design of attic or roof systems as does the applicable building code but neither limit the choice.

Text

 

Throughout the balance of this digest the terms attic and roof will and can be used interchangeably.

In cold climates, the primary purpose of attic or roof ventilation is to maintain a cold roof temperature to control ice dams created by melting snow, and to vent moisture that moves from the conditioned space to the attic (ventilation acts to bypass the vapour barrier created by most roof membranes). Melted snow, in this case, is caused by heat loss from the conditioned space. The heat loss is typically a combination of air leakage and conductive losses. The air leakage is due to exfiltration from the conditioned space (often because a ceiling air barrier is not present) and from leaky supply ductwork (often because ductwork located in attics is not well sealed) and from penetrations like non-airtight recessed lights. The conductive losses are usually from supply ductwork and equipment located in attic spaces ab

const tabId = 725789721;

// Click inside editor area
await tool.mouse({ action: "left_click", tabId, coordinate: [500, 300] });

// Select all and delete
await tool.press({ tabId, keys: "ControlOrMeta+a Backspace" });

// Memo text
const memoText = `DECISION MEMO: CLIMATE-CONTROLLED SHED INSULATION STRATEGIES
Target Structure: 10x12 Backyard Office / Workshop (120 sq. ft. Footprint, 590 sq. ft. Total Thermal Envelope)

1. EXECUTIVE DECISION SUMMARY
- BEST OVERALL OPTION: Strategy 2 - Mineral Wool (Rockwool Comfortbatt) + Continuous Rigid Foam Hybrid
  Why: Delivers superior thermal and acoustic performance (R-15 walls, R-25 ceiling, R-10 floor). Rockwool is noncombustible, hydrophobic (does not slump or rot when exposed to humidity), and friction-fits tightly. Continuous 2" XPS rigid foam on the ceiling breaks thermal bridging across rafters and forms an airtight vapor-retarder plane that stops warm indoor moisture from reaching the roof deck. Completely DIY-friendly with hand tools; zero hazardous chemical off-gassing. Material Cost: ~$1,154.

- BEST BUDGET OPTION: Strategy 1 - Traditional Vented Fiberglass Batt Assembly
  Why: Uses standard R-13 kraft-faced fiberglass in 2x4 walls, R-19 in 2x6 ceiling rafters with plastic ventilation baffles (Accuvent/Durovent), and R-13 in floor joists over a 6-mil poly ground barrier. Lowest upfront cost (~$485 - $550).
  Trade-offs: Moderate R-value, vulnerable to airflow degradation, slumps and harbors mold if exposed to moisture, attractive to rodents, and requires meticulous stapling and air sealing.

- OPTION TO AVOID: Strategy 3 - DIY Closed-Cell Spray Foam Kits (Froth-Pak / Touch 'n Foam)
  Why Avoid: Prohibitively expensive ($2,574 - $3,003 for 6-7 Froth-Pak 200 kits), high risk of catastrophic DIY application failure (substrate temperature sensitivity causes off-ratio chemical mixing, leaving gooey, foul-smelling, toxic un-cured foam that must be hand-scraped), exothermic fire hazard if sprayed >2" in a single pass, severe isocyanate fumes requiring full chemical PPE and respirators, and permanently conceals roof deck water leaks until structural rot occurs.

2. DETAILED COMPARISON OF 3 FULL INSULATION STRATEGIES

STRATEGY 1: Budget Fiberglass Batts with Vented Roof (Traditional Cavity Fill)
- Walls: 2x4 framing with R-13 kraft-faced fiberglass rolls/batts.
- Roof/Ceiling: 2x6 rafters with rafter baffles (1" air chute beneath deck) and R-19 fiberglass batts.
- Floor: 2x6 joists with R-13 batts held by wire stays + 6-mil poly ground vapor barrier.
- R-Value Approach: Walls R-13, Ceiling R-19, Floor R-13.
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Kraft paper facing on warm-in-winter side; soffit-to-ridge ventilation baffles prevent warm moist indoor exfiltration from condensing on the cold roof deck.
- Interior Space Consumed: 0" (sits flush inside stud and rafter cavities).
- DIY Difficulty: Low / Beginner (standard utility knife and stapler).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Fiberglass loses R-value if compressed or wet; crushed baffles cause roof deck rot; rodent nesting in floor cavities.

STRATEGY 2: Mineral Wool + Continuous Rigid Foam Hybrid (Recommended Winner)
- Walls: 2x4 framing filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt (3.5" friction-fit).
- Roof/Ceiling: Rafters filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt + continuous 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) fastened across rafter bottoms with Go Board washers/screws; seams taped with Tyvek/Sika tape and perimeter spray-foamed.
- Floor: 2x6 joists with 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) friction-fit between joists and sealed with canned foam, under 3/4" subfloor, plus 6-mil ground poly barrier.
- R-Value Approach: Walls R-15, Ceiling R-25 (R-15 batt + R-10 continuous XPS), Floor R-10.
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Rockwool is naturally hydrophobic; taped 2" rigid foam acts as an interior air barrier and Class II vapor retarder (<1.0 perm), eliminating condensation on framing.
- Interior Space Consumed: 2" loss of ceiling headroom; 0" loss on walls and floor.
- DIY Difficulty: Moderate (serrated insulation knife, straightedge for foam scoring, screw gun, seam taping).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Incomplete seam taping or perimeter foaming can allow air bypass; requires proper screw and washer spacing into rafters.

STRATEGY 3: Full Closed-Cell Spray Polyurethane Foam (ccSPF)
- Walls: 2" ccSPF sprayed directly onto exterior sheathing inside 2x4 bays (R-12.4).
- Roof/Ceiling: 3" ccSPF sprayed directly to the underside of the roof deck creating an unvented hot roof (R-18.6).
- Floor: 2" ccSPF sprayed into joist bays against subfloor (R-12.4).
- R-Value Approach: R-6.2 per inch. Walls R-12.4 (2"), Ceiling R-18.6 (3"), Floor R-12.4 (2").
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Self-flashing, air-impermeable, Class II vapor retarder at >=2" thickness. No ventilation chutes needed.
- Interior Space Consumed: 0" beyond framing cavity.
- DIY Difficulty: High / Hazardous (strict 65-80 deg F chemical temperature, full hazmat suit, organic vapor respirator, rapid 30-sec tip curing).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Off-ratio chemical mix results in toxic uncured goo; fire hazard from exothermic heat in thick passes; traps external leaks behind foam causing hidden roof deck decay.

3. PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION FOR A 10x12 CLIMATE-CONTROLLED SHED
- Wall Assembly: 2x4 framing @ 16" O.C. filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt (3.5" thickness), covered with interior 1/2" drywall or painted plywood.
- Roof/Ceiling Assembly: 2x6 rafters with upper vent chutes, filled with R-15 Rockwool batts, capped along rafter undersides by 2" Owens Corning Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) held by Go Board washers and 3" screws. All board seams taped with acrylic tape and perimeter-sealed with Great Stuff Window & Door foam, creating an airtight R-25 ceiling envelope.
- Floor Assembly: 2x6 pressure-treated floor framing set on skids/piers over a 6-mil polyethylene ground moisture sheet. 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) installed between joists and sealed at edges with canned foam; 3/4" tongue-and-groove OSB subfloor glued with construction adhesive.
- Climate Control Compatibility: Perfectly paired with a 9,000 BTU mini-split heat pump to maintain year-round temperature and actively dehumidify the conditioned space.

4. MATERIALS BASKET & ESTIMATED COST BREAKDOWN (10x12 SHED: 590 SQ. FT.)
- Strategy 1 (Budget Fiberglass):
  * Walls: 8 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced (40 sq ft/roll @ $27.97) = $223.76
  * Ceiling: 4 rolls Owens Corning R-19 Faced (~$35.00/roll) + 12 Accuvent Baffles ($5.98 ea) = $140.00 + $71.76 = $211.76
  * Floor: 3 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced ($83.91) + 6-mil poly ($22.00) + insulation wire stays ($18.00) = $123.91
  * Accessories: Staples and tape = $25.00
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$584.43

- Strategy 2 (Mineral Wool + Rigid Foam Hybrid - WINNER):
  * Walls: 6 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt (59.7 sq ft/bag @ $84.98) = $509.88
  * Ceiling: 3 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt ($254.94) + 5 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet = $299.85) = $554.79
  * Floor: 4 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet) = $239.88 + 6-mil poly ($22.00) = $261.88
  * Accessories: 2 cans Great Stuff Pro ($16.00), 1 roll Tyvek/Sika seam tape ($14.97), 1 box Go Board washers & screws ($24.00) = $54.97
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$1,381.52

- Strategy 3 (Full Closed-Cell Spray Foam Kit):
  * Board Feet Required: (320 sq ft walls * 2") + (120 sq ft floor * 2") + (150 sq ft ceiling * 3") = 1,330 board-ft.
  * Froth-Pak 200 Kits Required: 1,330 / 200 = 7 kits @ $429.00 = $3,003.00 (or 6 kits for 2" ceiling = $2,574.00)
  * Safety & PPE Gear: Full-face/half-mask organic vapor respirator, Tyvek suits, goggles, gloves = $120.00
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$2,694.00 - $3,123.00
`;

await tool.keyboard_insert_text({ tabId, text: memoText });

// Screenshot to verify
const ss = await browser.screenshot({ tabId });
console.log("Screenshot after memo insert:", ss.image);

- DIY Difficulty: Moderate (serrated insulation knife, straightedge for foam scoring, screw gun, seam taping).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Incomplete seam taping or perimeter foaming can allow air bypass; requires proper screw and washer spacing into rafters.

STRATEGY 3: Full Closed-Cell Spray Polyurethane Foam (ccSPF)
- Walls: 2" ccSPF sprayed directly onto exterior sheathing inside 2x4 bays (R-12.4).
- Roof/Ceiling: 3" ccSPF sprayed directly to the underside of the roof deck creating an unvented hot roof (R-18.6).
- Floor: 2" ccSPF sprayed into joist bays against subfloor (R-12.4).
- R-Value Approach: R-6.2 per inch. Walls R-12.4 (2"), Ceiling R-18.6 (3"), Floor R-12.4 (2").
- Moisture/Vapor Control: Self-flashing, air-impermeable, Class II vapor retarder at >=2" thickness. No ventilation chutes needed.
- Interior Space Consumed: 0" beyond framing cavity.
- DIY Difficulty: High / Hazardous (strict 65-80 deg F chemical temperature, full hazmat suit, organic vapor respirator, rapid 30-sec tip curing).
- Failure Risks / Watch-outs: Off-ratio chemical mix results in toxic uncured goo; fire hazard from exothermic heat in thick passes; traps external leaks behind foam causing hidden roof deck decay.

3. PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION FOR A 10x12 CLIMATE-CONTROLLED SHED
- Wall Assembly: 2x4 framing @ 16" O.C. filled with R-15 Rockwool Comfortbatt (3.5" thickness), covered with interior 1/2" drywall or painted plywood.
- Roof/Ceiling Assembly: 2x6 rafters with upper vent chutes, filled with R-15 Rockwool batts, capped along rafter undersides by 2" Owens Corning Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) held by Go Board washers and 3" screws. All board seams taped with acrylic tape and perimeter-sealed with Great Stuff Window & Door foam, creating an airtight R-25 ceiling envelope.
- Floor Assembly: 2x6 pressure-treated floor framing set on skids/piers over a 6-mil polyethylene ground moisture sheet. 2" Foamular NGX XPS (R-10) installed between joists and sealed at edges with canned foam; 3/4" tongue-and-groove OSB subfloor glued with construction adhesive.
- Climate Control Compatibility: Perfectly paired with a 9,000 BTU mini-split heat pump to maintain year-round temperature and actively dehumidify the conditioned space.

4. MATERIALS BASKET & ESTIMATED COST BREAKDOWN (10x12 SHED: 590 SQ. FT.)
- Strategy 1 (Budget Fiberglass):
  * Walls: 8 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced (40 sq ft/roll @ $27.97) = $223.76
  * Ceiling: 4 rolls Owens Corning R-19 Faced (~$35.00/roll) + 12 Accuvent Baffles ($5.98 ea) = $140.00 + $71.76 = $211.76
  * Floor: 3 rolls Owens Corning R-13 Faced ($83.91) + 6-mil poly ($22.00) + insulation wire stays ($18.00) = $123.91
  * Accessories: Staples and tape = $25.00
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$584.43

- Strategy 2 (Mineral Wool + Rigid Foam Hybrid - WINNER):
  * Walls: 6 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt (59.7 sq ft/bag @ $84.98) = $509.88
  * Ceiling: 3 bags Rockwool R-15 Comfortbatt ($254.94) + 5 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet = $299.85) = $554.79
  * Floor: 4 sheets Foamular NGX 2" XPS R-10 4x8 ($59.97/sheet) = $239.88 + 6-mil poly ($22.00) = $261.88
  * Accessories: 2 cans Great Stuff Pro ($16.00), 1 roll Tyvek/Sika seam tape ($14.97), 1 box Go Board washers & screws ($24.00) = $54.97
  * TOTAL ESTIMATED COST: ~$1,381.52

- Strategy 3 (Full Closed-Cell Spray Foam Kit):
  * Board Feet Required: (320 sq ft walls * 2") + (120 sq ft floor * 2") + (150 sq ft ceiling * 3") = 1,330 board-ft.
  * Froth-Pak 200 Kits Required: 1,330 / 200 = 7 kits @ $429.00 = $3,003.00 (or 6 kits for 2" ceiling = $2,574.00)

Practical Recommendation for a 10x12 Climate-Controlled Shed For a standard 10x12 outbuilding (120 sq. ft. floor, ~320 net sq. ft. walls, ~150 sq. ft. roof/ceiling), the ideal year-round climate-controlled assembly that balances thermal resistance, airtightness, acoustic isolation, and DIY buildability is **Strategy 2 (Mineral Wool + Rigid Foam Hybrid)**. ### A. Recommended Wall Assembly - **Framing:** Standard 2x4 framing at 16" on-center. - **Exterior Weather Barrier:** Exterior sheathing (OSB or plywood) wrapped with a water-resistive barrier (DuPont Tyvek HomeWrap) with taped seams, behind standard siding on rainscreen furring strips (or direct-applied siding). - **Cavity Insulation:** **ROCKWOOL Comfortbatt R-15** (3.5" thickness, 15" width). Friction-fit firmly between studs with no gaps or compression. - **Interior Finish:** 1/2" drywall (taped and primed with vapor-retardant latex paint) or 1/2" interior plywood. An interior 6-mil poly sheet should be **omitted** to prevent a double vapor barrier that traps summer humidity. ### B. Recommended Roof / Ceiling Assembly - **Framing:** 2x6 roof rafters at 16" or 24" on-center. - **Ventilation:** Continuous vented soffit at the eaves connected to upper gable louvers or a continuous ridge vent. Install **Amerimax Accuvent** baffles (or Durovent) in every rafter bay against the roof deck to guarantee a 1" to 1.5" continuous air channel. - **Cavity Insulation:** **ROCKWOOL Comfortbatt R-15** installed below the baffles within the rafter bays. - **Continuous Thermal Break & Air Barrier:** **2" Owens Corning FOAMULAR NGX F-250 XPS (R-10)** panels fastened directly across the underside of the rafters using 3" construction screws through 1.25" Go Board / plastic insulation washers. - **Air Sealing:** Seal all board perimeter perimeters and penetrations with low-expansion Great Stuff Pro Window & Door polyurethane foam, and tape all board butt-joints with DuPont Tyvek Acrylic Construction Tape. This creates an airtight, continuous interior ceiling plane providing **R-25 total resistance** and completely stopping warm, humid indoor air from reaching the cold roof deck. ### C. Recommended Floor Assembly - **Sub-Base:** Ground cleared and sloped away from the shed, covered with a heavy **6-mil polyethylene sheet** ballasted with gravel to stop rising ground moisture. Pier blocks or skids elevate the shed floor framing at least 6" off the ground for cross-ventilation. - **Framing:** Pressure-treated 2x6 floor joists at 16" on-center. - **Insulation:** **2" Owens Corning FOAMULAR NGX XPS (R-10)** rigid foam boards cut to width and friction-fitted between the joists, supported by 1x2 ledger strips or corrosion-resistant screws. Seal all perimeter gaps between foam and joists with canned expanding foam to block air infiltration and rodent intrusion. - **Subfloor:** 3/4" tongue-and-groove exterior-grade OSB or plywood glued to the joists with subfloor construction adhesive (e.g., Liquid Nails) and screwed down. - **Finished Floor:** Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) with integrated waterproof underlayment. ### D. Climate Control Pairing Pair this tight envelope with an appropriately sized **9,000 BTU mini-split heat pump** (or a dual-hose inverter window heat pump). In a 120 sq. ft. space with an R-15/R-25/R-10 envelope, a mini-split will operate at minimum modulation, maintain exact workspace temperatures in sub-freezing winters or hot summers, and actively dehumidify the air to eliminate indoor moisture accumulation. --- ## 4.
